# Introduction {#sec-intro}

In most statistical and machine learning literature, datasets are assumed to be complete, regular, and unfragmented. In short, most models assume complete data for processing. However, in the real domain, a lot of datasets are incomplete, irregular, and fragmented. This is particularly evident in the medical and biomedical domain, where collection of datasets are dependent on the availability of patients and the robustness of wet lab experiments, which are not always 100% reliable.

In this chapter, we will introduce the different types of missingness that has been proposed in the literature, as well as propose a new classification of missingness based on a different perspective. We will also discuss how the semi-supervised setting can be viewed as a special case of missing data, and how it can be incorporated into the overall missingness framework.

## Problem Formulation

Throughout this thesis I will adopt notation similar to @hyperimpute for the problem formulation and denote missing values as `NaN`. Let $\bm{X}\in\mathbb{R}^D$ be a D-dimensional random vector.

## Types of missingness

Classical literature mainly distinguishes three main missingness mechanisms depending on the relationship between the probability of missingness with the observed and unobserved data [@typesOfMissingness]. 

### \acr{MCAR}

\acr{MCAR} is a missingness mechanism where the probability of missingness is independent of the observed and unobserved data. In other words, the missingness is completely random and does not depend on any of the observed or unobserved data.
